title: SIM-GRAPH: A universal guide to symmetric interactions
authors: R. C. Verstraten, C. Morais Smith
abstract: Symmetry plays a central role throughout physics, from Fourier analysis on discrete lattices to the classification of elementary particles in the standard model. In finite quantum systems, symmetries are often discrete, such as reflection and rotational symmetries. Here, we present the SIM-GRAPH method (Symmetric Ising Models - Graph Reduction And Projected Hamiltonians), which uses such symmetries to efficiently calculate ground-state observables of interacting quantum systems. By projecting all interactions onto a symmetric subset of the system, the method effectively reduces the number of sites, thus providing an exponential speedup over standard exact diagonalization. Furthermore, we introduce two extensions that broaden the applicability of the method and allow for a controlled trade-off between computational cost and accuracy.
summary: This paper introduces SIM-GRAPH, a novel method that leverages underlying symmetries in quantum Hamiltonians to drastically reduce the computational complexity of finding ground-state properties. By projecting the system onto a symmetry-reduced graph, it achieves exponential speedups over standard exact diagonalization for models like the TFIM. This makes the study of large, complex quantum magnetic systems computationally feasible.
main_problem: The primary challenge is efficiently calculating ground-state observables for interacting quantum many-body systems, which typically suffer from exponential scaling when using exact diagonalization.
main_result: The SIM-GRAPH method provides an exponential speedup by projecting interactions onto a symmetry-reduced graph, allowing for the study of large systems previously intractable.
method: The method uses group theory to identify symmetries, reducing the system Hamiltonian by projecting interactions onto a smaller, symmetric subset of the lattice sites, resulting in a reduced Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The method is applied to interacting quantum spin systems, specifically using the Transverse Field Ising Model (TFIM) on various lattices, including 1D chains, 2D square lattices, and Sierpinski triangles.
key_observables: Ground-state observables, such as average magnetization ($\langle n_{\uparrow} angle$) and ground-state energy.
important_parameters: The size and geometry of the lattice (e.g., 3x3, 4x4, 1D chains); the symmetry group $S$ used for reduction.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the ground-state observables are not significantly affected by spontaneous symmetry breaking, and that the lowest energy symmetric state is sufficient for accurate results.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the graph reduction process for lattices (e.g., 3x3 square lattice, 1D chain), comparing results from Exact Diagonalization (ED) against SIM-GRAPH variants ($	ext{SIM}1, 	ext{SIM}2.1, 	ext{SIM}2.4$) for magnetization.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the core SIM-GRAPH technique, details its extensions (SIM2 for superpositions, SIM3 for partial symmetries), and validates its performance across various geometries (1D, 2D, Sierpinski) by comparing results against ED benchmarks.
why_interesting: The technique provides a powerful, symmetry-based computational shortcut for strongly correlated models, offering insights into how symmetries constrain the low-energy physics of magnetic materials.

The three dis- tinct symmetric representations Si are highlighted in red on the left hand side. On the right hand side, we see the reduced graph, where all interactions are projected to the symmetric subset and the other sites are removed. The remaining sites are relabeled to a counting order.

FIG. 2. The average ground-state magnetization of the TFIM on the 3 × 3 square lattice is presented at V/Ω= 10 for both NN and VdW interactions, computed using both ED and SIM-GRAPH. For better visual comparison, the exact results are plotted using larger points, with the SIM-GRAPH results overlaid in points half the size. For both NN and VdW interactions, we find excellent agreement with only minor de- viations from the exact results.

FIG. 3. The average ground-state magnetization of the TFIM on the 4 × 4 square lattice is presented at V/Ω= 10 for both NN and VdW interactions, computed on 50 points using both ED and SIM-GRAPH. For both NN and VdW interactions, we find deviations up to 4 spins away from the exact results. Besides the high and low ∆/Ωlimits, we find only one region of agreement at ⟨n↑⟩= 8, which corresponds to the checker- board states.
